headline: Anthropic unveils Model Hardware Standard to control physical devices with AI
summary: The new standard aims to simplify device integration for AI agents, reducing setup time from months to minutes and enabling AI to control physical experiments.
details: Anthropic has introduced the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a set of standardized drivers designed to allow AI agents to interface with and control physical devices. This innovation moves AI beyond the digital realm of text, images, and code into direct interaction with the physical world.

Currently in a "research preview," MHS is positioned to help scientists streamline the creation of custom software integrations for experiments. By providing a common interface and data format, MHS enables disparate devices to communicate without bespoke translator programs, potentially cutting down experimental setup time from weeks or months to hours or minutes.

The inspiration for MHS reportedly came from observing a neuroscientist's complex experiment, highlighting the need for a common interface to coordinate various components like laser beams, microscopes, and cameras. This concept could be extended to allow AI to run virtually any scientific experiment.

While MHS devices can be controlled directly via command-line or API, integration with AI models via the Model Context Protocol allows for natural language interaction. This enables AI models to reason through experimental steps, adjust parameters in real-time, and even recover from hardware errors autonomously.

Anthropic demonstrated how an AI model like Claude could use MHS to adjust a laser, analyze results with a camera, and calibrate a system, or focus a microscope and automatically move it to relevant sections for further observation.

In one example, Claude was shown using MHS to figure out how to pick up an aluminum can with a robotic arm, even without specific prior training for that task. MHS-enabled models can also sequence steps across instruments by writing and adjusting API scripts as needed.

MHS includes a standardized tagging system to describe hardware constraints, such as a robot arm's weight and range, adjustable parameters, and safety limits. This information is integrated into a reference file, providing AI models with crucial data about unfamiliar devices.

Anthropic is currently collaborating with scientific research labs and advanced manufacturers, including AWS, Hugging Face, Raspberry Pi, Automata, and Universal Robots, during the MHS preview period. These partners will aid in developing safety evaluations and best practices for AI operating physical equipment.

The long-term plan is for MHS to become an open-source, agent-agnostic standard for integrating AI and physical systems. Early testing has already shown MHS reducing device integration time and enabling faster iteration in experimental settings, potentially accelerating the development of general technologies.
